clinicalPearls: A bilateral chronic posterior uveitis typically affecting middle-aged adults, with a strong female predominance
Extremely strong association with HLA-A29, one of the tightest HLA-disease links known, supporting testing when the diagnosis is considered
Named for multiple cream-coloured, ovoid choroidal lesions radiating from the optic disc in a pattern resembling birdshot from a shotgun
Patients often report symptoms disproportionate to acuity, including nyctalopia, floaters, colour disturbance and difficulty in dim light despite relatively preserved central vision
Vitritis is usually present but with characteristically minimal anterior segment inflammation
Cystoid macular oedema is the leading cause of visual loss and a key treatment target
Indocyanine green angiography reveals hypofluorescent choroidal lesions that are often more numerous than those seen clinically
Management principles rely on long-term systemic immunosuppression, with corticosteroids for acute control and steroid-sparing agents for maintenance
reference.pathophysiology: Birdshot chorioretinopathy is an organ-specific autoimmune inflammation of the choroid and retina, occurring almost exclusively in genetically predisposed HLA-A29-positive individuals. An autoreactive T-cell response, possibly directed against retinal antigens, drives multifocal granulomatous infiltration of the choroid, producing the characteristic depigmented birdshot lesions. Associated retinal vasculitis and breakdown of the blood-retinal barrier lead to cystoid macular oedema, while progressive photoreceptor and retinal pigment epithelial dysfunction cause the electroretinographic abnormalities and night-vision loss. Chronic inflammation results in choroidal and retinal atrophy over time.
additionalInvestigations: HLA-A29 typing to support the diagnosis in the appropriate clinical setting
Indocyanine green angiography to detect hypofluorescent choroidal lesions
Fluorescein angiography to demonstrate retinal vasculitis, disc leakage and cystoid macular oedema
Optical coherence tomography to monitor macular oedema and photoreceptor integrity
Electroretinography to assess and track retinal functional decline
Visual field testing to detect peripheral field loss disproportionate to acuity
redFlags: Progressive cystoid macular oedema threatening central vision despite treatment
Deteriorating electroretinogram indicating widespread retinal dysfunction
Features atypical for the diagnosis raising concern for intraocular lymphoma
Development of choroidal neovascularisation or optic atrophy
reference.prognosis: Birdshot chorioretinopathy is a chronic, relapsing disease; with sustained immunosuppression many patients maintain good central vision, but untreated or poorly controlled disease leads to progressive macular oedema, retinal atrophy and irreversible loss of night vision, colour vision and peripheral field.
pitfalls: Relying on central acuity alone and underestimating functional loss from field and night-vision impairment
Discontinuing immunosuppression prematurely because acuity appears stable
Missing a vitreoretinal lymphoma masquerading as birdshot uveitis
Assuming a negative HLA-A29 result excludes the diagnosis in an otherwise classic case
Neglecting objective monitoring with electroretinography and angiography when relying on symptoms alone
management: Systemic corticosteroids to gain initial control, transitioning to steroid-sparing immunosuppression with antimetabolites, calcineurin inhibitors or biologic agents for durable suppression
Target cystoid macular oedema, the leading cause of visual loss, with local or systemic anti-inflammatory therapy
Consider periocular or intravitreal corticosteroid for refractory macular oedema
Surveillance with optical coherence tomography, electroretinography and visual fields to track inflammation and retinal function
Use HLA-A29 typing and indocyanine green angiography to support diagnosis and monitor choroidal lesions
Manage under a uveitis or medical-retina specialist, escalating immunosuppression for progressive electroretinographic decline or recurrent oedema
